prime.problem: Twenty-one algorithms look like twenty-one things to memorise. Without a map you can't tell which one a new problem wants, or why the fast one is allowed to skip work, so in an interview you reach for whatever you practised last.
prime.fits: The front door of course 2. It builds on cs-1's big-O and heaps, and folds every card here into one formula: passes × work per pass, and three ways to cut it.
expect: halve · never back up · don't compare
what makes a shortcut safe: invariant, monotone test, exchange argument
prime.goal: Given a new problem, name the family it belongs to, the term of the formula the fast algorithm cuts, and the argument that makes the cut safe.

attend: For each of the three ways to cut work (halve, never back up, don't compare), which cards use it, and which term of passes × work does it shrink?
Why can merge sort get within 8% of log₂ n! compares but never under it, while radix sort ignores the floor completely?
Which rows of the "wrong → right" table are measured timings and which are counted steps, and why does the page warn against reading counted ratios as speed?
What do an invariant, a monotone yes/no test and an exchange argument each let an algorithm throw away?
When does the page say to use the built-in (sorted(), s.find, np.partition) instead of the card's algorithm?

must: Cost = passes × work per pass → halving what's left makes passes log₂ n (binary search, merge sort, D&C) → a one-way sweep makes it one pass of ≤ 2n pointer moves (two pointers, KMP, Manacher) → reading keys instead of comparing escapes the compare count altogether (radix, hashing)

Compare-only sorting must tell n! orders apart → each yes/no halves them at best → at least log₂ n! ≈ n log₂ n compares (18,488,885 for 10⁶) → only an algorithm that looks inside the keys can go under it

A shortcut throws work away → it is only correct if something proves the thrown-away part can't hold the answer → invariant (lo/hi, tails), monotone predicate, or exchange argument → no proof, no shortcut (greedy coins {1, 3, 4} for 6 fails)

Big-O counts steps, not seconds → constants and language decide real time (np.sort 0.031 s vs sorted() 0.130 s, both n log n) → in Python the built-in in C usually wins → write the algorithm for a guarantee or an interview
elevated: Worst case vs expected: quicksort, quickselect and rolling hash are fast only in expectation over their own random choices → an adversary who knows a fixed pivot or a fixed (B, p) can force the bad case → heapsort, KMP and Manacher promise the worst case
reference: the log-scale speedup bars and their exact ratios
CLRS chapter numbers and the listsort.txt / numpy links

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the course's causal map: the formula passes × work per pass in the middle, three arrows out of it (halve, never back up, don't compare) each ending in 2–3 card names, the log₂ n! floor as a wall that only "don't compare" crosses, and underneath, the three proofs that make a shortcut safe.
checklist: cost = passes × work per pass, and each fast algorithm cuts one term
halve → log n passes: binary search, merge sort, divide and conquer, quickselect's shrinking work
never back up → ≤ 2n pointer moves: two pointers, KMP, Manacher
don't compare → escape log₂ n!: radix, rolling hash, array as its own hash
safety comes from an invariant, a monotone test or an exchange argument
Big-O is steps; built-ins in C often win in Python

retrieve.q: Explain why "sorted in O(n)" is impossible for a sort that only compares, yet LSD radix sort does it for fixed-width integers. Name the assumption radix breaks.
answer: compare-only: n! orders, each compare at best halves them → ≥ log₂ n! compares
radix never asks x < y; it reads digits, so the decision-tree argument doesn't apply
the price: keys must be fixed-width (d passes), and it needs O(n + w) extra memory

retrieve.q: Walk through how the page gets 20,000,000, 18,488,885 and 4,001,024 for sorting 10⁶ keys, and what kind of step each number counts.
answer: floor: log₂(10⁶!) compares, for any compare sort
radix, w = 256, 32-bit keys: 4 passes × (10⁶ + 256) bucket moves, no compares
different units, so compare them as orders of magnitude, not timings

retrieve.q: A teammate replaces sorted() with a hand-written quicksort "because it's O(n log n) too" and random-pivot quicksort beats merge sort in C. What does the page say they lose, and when would a hand-written algorithm be justified?
answer: pure Python loses to C: insertion sort vs sorted() was ≈ 3,200× on 5,000 items, much of it bytecode vs C
they lose stability and Timsort's O(n) on already-sorted runs
write your own only for a guarantee the built-in lacks (linear worst case, a stream) or in an interview

compare.q: cs-1's big-O card and this map both talk about cost. What does this course add on top of "count the steps", and where does big-O alone mislead you here?
answer: this course asks which term to cut (passes or work per pass) and why the cut is safe
big-O hides constants: np.sort 0.031 s vs sorted() 0.130 s at the same n log n
and it hides worst vs expected: quicksort's O(n log n) is an average; a fixed pivot on sorted input is n(n − 1)/2

compare.q: Greedy and divide and conquer end this course; DP starts the next. Which failure of each paradigm sends you to DP?
answer: greedy fails when no exchange or lower-bound proof exists: coins {1, 3, 4} for 6 gives 3 coins, DP finds 2
divide and conquer blows up when subproblems overlap (naive Fibonacci) → memoize them
DP keeps every subproblem's answer instead of committing (greedy) or recomputing (naive recursion)

predict.q: The "wrong → right" table shows a 50,000× gain from bisecting d in k-th pair distance. Predict what happens to that ratio if values only go up to 10³ instead of 10⁶ (n still 10⁴). Bigger, smaller, or the same?
predict.answer: Smaller. Trying d = 0, 1, 2 … needs up to W + 1 passes and bisecting needs ⌈log₂(W + 1)⌉ passes. At W = 10⁶ that's 10⁶ + 1 vs 20 (≈ 50,000×). At W = 10³ it's 1,001 vs ⌈log₂ 1,001⌉ = 10, only about 100×. Halving pays most when the answer space is huge.

apply.task: Redo the page's sort budget for n = 10⁵ instead of 10⁶, by hand: (1) merge sort passes and element copies, (2) the compare floor (use the card value log₂(10⁵!) ≈ 1,516,704), (3) LSD radix with w = 256 on 32-bit keys. Then say which cut each one makes (fewer passes, less work per pass, or no compares).
apply.done: You have three numbers and one sentence each, and they match: 17 passes × 10⁵ = 1,700,000 copies; ≈ 1,516,704 compares at least; 4 × (10⁵ + 256) = 401,024 bucket moves.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: did you expect the pair-distance speedup to hold at any W?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the floor stops merge sort but not radix sort?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: shortcut → proof of safety, or proof → which part can be thrown away?
Which family (sorting, binary search, linear scans, strings, paradigms) do you feel least able to pick out of a problem statement?
Which card will you open first, and what one question will you read it for?
